question: A caller says he is from your bank's fraud team and your savings are at risk. Which of these prove he is real?
answer: Only what you reach yourself. Everything a caller can show you, he can buy or fake: leaked names and addresses, a spoofed number, a sender name on a text. That is why banks say they will never ask you to move money to a safe account. The request alone tells you who is calling.
move: Trust the line you opened, never the one that opened you.
ask: Which of my accounts could a calm, well-informed stranger talk me out of in one phone call?

items.note: He knows your full name and home address.
items.verdict: Leaked in data breaches and sold by the million. Anyone can buy it.

items.note: The number on your screen matches the one on your card.
items.verdict: Caller ID can be faked: the number shown is whatever the caller types.

items.note: He reads out the last four digits of your card.
items.verdict: They are printed on receipts and shown in online shops. Many scammers have them.

items.note: His text arrives among your bank's real messages.
items.verdict: A text's sender name can be faked too, so it files itself with the real ones.

items.note: His link opens a site with a padlock in the address bar.
items.verdict: The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.

items.note: You hang up and dial the number on your card yourself.
items.verdict: Now you chose who answers. Use another phone if you can: a line can be held open.

items.note: The same alert is there when you open the bank's app yourself.
items.verdict: You went in through a door you trust. A link sent to you would not count.

source: UK Finance, Take Five to Stop Fraud
reference: https://www.takefive-stopfraud.org.uk/ ; Ofcom, Tackling scam calls and texts, 2022
